issues.explanation: For a 68-year-old married man whose index trauma was a life-threatening accident, 'kids crying' and 'physical affection such as hugs' are difficult to reconcile as principal trauma triggers given the rest of the profile. The memory, appraisal, threat, and coping items all center on bodily pain, fragmented accident memory, hypervigilance, self-blame, and safety behaviors, but do not provide a plausible bridge from an accident trauma to these interpersonal/child-related triggers.

The other triggers and symptoms center on danger, bodily pain, alcohol smell, vigilance, and fragmented accident memory; affection-based triggering suggests an interpersonal/assault-related pattern that is not otherwise represented.

'Avoid Police' is weakly coherent with the stated trauma type and with the rest of the profile. Nothing in the triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals points to police involvement, legal aftermath, or authority-related danger. In an accident case this would be possible, but here it appears disconnected enough to question whether it belongs to the same formulation.

vignette:
Thomas Weber is a 68-year-old American politician of European background who came to treatment after many months of trying to contain the aftermath of a serious car accident on his own. He is married and has spent decades moving through public life with a practiced sense of steadiness, but since the accident he has felt that steadiness give way in ways that are hard for him to hide and harder still for him to understand.

The accident happened while he was being driven back from an evening political event. There had been alcohol at the function, and although Thomas had not been driving, the smell of liquor lingered on guests, in handshakes, in the close air of the reception, and then again on the clothing he carried into the car. On the road home, another vehicle struck them hard. What remains with him is not a smooth story but a sequence of brutal stills: the sudden sight of another car coming into them, the impact, the interior of the vehicle jolting sideways, the sensation of his body taking the blow in specific places, and the sick certainty in those seconds that he might die there. When he tries to describe the crash aloud, he often starts, stops, loses the thread, and then gives up in frustration. He says it is as if he has only a few pictures in his mind and nothing that properly joins them together.

In the weeks after the collision, Thomas expected himself to recover with discipline. Instead, the event kept returning in sharply bounded moments. If he saw footage of cars smashed at an intersection on the evening news, or passed an accident scene in a campaign vehicle, he felt himself pulled back to those images of impact. The smell of alcohol was especially potent. At fundraisers, receptions, and donor dinners, a whiff of whiskey or wine on someone’s breath could make his whole body tense before he had fully registered why. Along with the memory came pain in the same parts of his body that had been hurt in the crash, as though the event were being replayed not only in his mind but physically.

He became increasingly unwilling to drive, and then unwilling even to ride as a passenger unless absolutely necessary. For a man whose work depended on constant travel between offices, public meetings, and community events, this changed the shape of his days. He began finding reasons to attend fewer in-person appearances, asking staff to rearrange travel, preferring virtual meetings whenever he could. When he did have to get into a car, he was visibly uncomfortable, scanning the road, bracing at intersections, and staying preoccupied with what might happen next. He did not present this to others as fear; to himself, it felt more like necessity. He had come to believe that he had to be on guard all the time.

At home, nights became unsettled. Thomas would wake and check whether he was safe, orienting himself to the room and the house before he could lie back down. Silence also began to trouble him. He found ordinary quiet—late at night, in a paused meeting before someone spoke, in the stillness of a car before departure—strangely menacing, as if danger were gathering in the absence of sound. During the day he noticed his concentration slipping. In policy briefings and conversations with aides, he sometimes found his attention breaking apart, which he experienced as humiliating in a role where command of detail had always been central to his identity.

What disturbed him most was not only the persistence of these reactions but what he believed they said about him. Thomas repeatedly turned the accident over in his mind, dwelling on what he had done wrong and blaming himself without reaching any relief. His self-reproach was broad and cutting: the event happened, he felt, because of the sort of person he was. He could not fully articulate why that conclusion felt true, but it carried emotional force. In public he became acutely self-conscious, convinced that other people could see what had happened to him just by looking at him. Standing at podiums, walking corridors at the capitol, or greeting constituents, he felt exposed, as though his injury and fear had become visible features he could no longer control.

His wife had watched him narrow his world, sleep poorly, and return from obligatory car rides tense and depleted. The immediate reason he finally agreed to seek help was a recent campaign-related trip during which he caught the smell of alcohol on a supporter as he was being ushered into a car, then froze when traffic slowed beside a wrecked vehicle on the shoulder. Later that night he woke repeatedly to check the room and could not return to sleep. He came to treatment troubled by how small and vigilant his life had become, frightened that he could no longer trust himself in the settings his work requires, and hoping, cautiously, that he might find a way to be in cars, in public, and in quiet rooms without feeling that danger is already there.
